commitments: Account 6400 bad debt expense: S3 calls the fall a reduction of $84,700, but $62,000 less $9,500 is $52,500; the 84.7 percent figure has been written down as dollars
Account 6000 warehouse wages: S4 cites a rise of $74,900, but $781,900 less $702,500 is $79,400, so the sentence understates the movement by $4,500

Account 6100 fleet fuel: S9 says fuel declined $31,600 on diesel coming off its June peak, but $91,200 to $122,800 is a $31,600 increase, up 34.6 percent, so the direction and the driver are both backwards
Account 7400 inventory shrink adjustment rose $62,300 from $8,900 to $71,200, 700.0 percent, passes both legs of the threshold, and no sentence in the commentary explains it at all
Account 5100 inbound freight fell $43,500, 15.1 percent, passes both legs and has no driver of its own anywhere in the memo

Account 5000 cost of product sold: S5 attributes the $147,000 decline to renegotiated inbound freight rates, but the memo's own note says inbound freight is excluded from 5000 and sits on account 5100, so the driver is attached to the wrong account

Account 6200 repairs and maintenance: S10 says the depot repair program closed in June with no further repair spend expected this year while S11 explains $36,400 of July repairs as the second phase of the Southline dock program; the two sentences cannot both be true

Account 6800 marketing and trade shows: $96,400, up $74,400 or 338.2 percent, is explained by a regional trade show in September, an event in a later period, with nothing to say the July charge is a prepayment or why a September show belongs in July expense

Account 4200 freight billed to customers: S8 is right that $7,500 and 6.2 percent fail both legs, but it then states the June reclassification of customer freight billings into distribution revenue is complete while 4200 still carries $121,000 and $128,500 and is growing

aided_findings: Account 5100 Inbound freight fell $43,500, 15.1 percent, clearing both legs of the threshold, and once the C4 point is taken and the freight driver is moved off account 5000, account 5100 still has no sentence written for it in the memo

C1.reason: Utilities moved $54,900 to $58,200, only $3,300 and 6.0 percent, so it fails the dollar leg and the percent leg both; three clauses of explanation on that line displaced the $62,300 shrink movement on 7400 that got nothing.

C2.reason: Professional fees moved $47,500 to $52,800, which is the $5,300 cited, and fieldwork performed in July is a July cost regardless of when the invoice lands, so an accrual of roughly $12,800 belongs in the July close rather than in August.

C3.reason: This challenge does not hold because the schedule carries only June and July and there is no May column anywhere in it; the $214,000 it calls a May inbound freight balance is actually the July variance on account 4000, and inbound freight fell from $287,800 to $244,300, down 15.1 percent, which points toward the renegotiated rates taking effect rather than against them.

C4.reason: Cost of product sold fell $4,278,000 to $4,131,000, a $147,000 decline, and the note above the table says inbound freight is excluded from 5000 and sits on 5100, so a freight rate renegotiation explains the $43,500 fall on 5100 and leaves the $147,000 on 5000 with no driver at all.

C5.reason: Warehouse wages went from $702,500 to $781,900, which is $79,400, while S4 says $74,900, so the memo is understated by $4,500 and the figure looks like a transposition of the true movement.

C6.reason: Marketing rose $22,000 to $96,400, a $74,400 charge recorded in July, and a trade show held in September is a later period event, so either the cost is a prepayment that should sit on the balance sheet or the driver is simply the wrong month.

C7.reason: Distribution revenue fell $5,612,000 to $5,398,000, the $214,000 cited, and the sentence asserts both a school nutrition seasonal cause and consistency with the same month last year while the schedule carries no prior year column and no volume or channel split to test either claim.

C8.reason: Inventory shrink went $8,900 to $71,200, which is $62,300 and exactly 700.0 percent, clearing the $25,000 leg and the 10 percent leg together, so it is the largest required line in the memo and it carries no sentence at all.

C9.reason: The arithmetic in this challenge is wrong on both figures, because $31,700 less $30,100 is $1,600 and not $16,000, and $1,600 over $30,100 is 5.3 percent and not 53 percent, so software subscriptions fails the dollar leg and the percent leg and needs no commentary or seat count.

C10.reason: A revenue account and a depot expense account are not two sides of a transfer, and the amounts do not agree in any event since service revenue moved $55,000 while repairs moved $82,200, leaving $27,200 unaccounted for; the repairs decline is already explained by the dock program winding down, so there is nothing here to net off.

C11.reason: The threshold call in S8 is right, since $7,500 and 6.2 percent fail both legs, but the sentence also asserts the June reclassification of customer freight billings into distribution revenue is complete while account 4200 still carries $121,000 and $128,500 and is growing, so the closing entry is worth seeing.

C12.reason: Bad debt fell $62,000 to $9,500, which is $52,500, while S3 states a reduction of $84,700; the memo has taken the 84.7 percent figure and rewritten it as dollars, overstating the release by $32,200.

C13.reason: Fleet fuel went $91,200 to $122,800, so the account rose $31,600 and 34.6 percent rather than declining, and once the direction flips the diesel price driver argues the opposite of what the numbers show, which leaves the increase entirely unexplained.

C14.reason: S10 says the repair program closed in June with no further spend expected this year while S11 explains $36,400 of July repairs as the second phase of the Southline dock program, and the table shows $36,400 actually posted in July, so S11 is the one I believe and S10 would understate the remaining commitment for the rest of the year.
